item.title: Claude or ChatGPT for code: 4 models on identical tasks
item.description:
Claude or ChatGPT for code: on eight identical tasks, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, ChatGPT 6 Astra, and ChatGPT 6.1 Sol wrote correct code on the first try, with one response only needing reformatting. The difference was found in response time (8 to 28 minutes for all tasks), price per token (up to 5x), and solution design. Read more

item.title: Shadow AI: Shut Down Support, Users Can Do It Themselves
item.description:
An employee encountered an error, copied it into a neural network, and it fixed everything for them. In half a minute, they were back to work, and no ticket or record of the interaction remained in the system. We explore what IT support loses in this scenario, why such self-service is particularly costly in Russia, and how to regain visibility without forcing people back into queues.

item.title: The Gray Wall of Singularity
item.description:
Technological singularity is usually discussed as a point after which artificial intelligence will discover new laws, create technologies, and improve its own models at such a speed that humans will be left to use the results of its work. Today, most of the devices around us seem almost magical to those unfamiliar with their workings. But within this "magic" are principles, research, calculations, and engineering solutions understandable to humans. At the same time, no single person holds all knowledge in their head. It exists as a common heritage of many scientists and specialists, which is transmitted, verified, and developed. Science, long before the advent of AI, became a collective way of understanding the world. What if the main result of AI development also enters this common pool of knowledge? Imagine that artificial intelligence helps discover a mathematical theory that is understandable to humans but also profound. One that makes previously separate areas of mathematics visible as parts of a single structure. Prepared specialists will be able to master its principles and apply them independently. And if the new theory simultaneously provides a significant advantage in already known calculations, the distribution of influence among people in society will change first and foremost. Read the article

item.title: One Hour in a World Without AI Agents: From Tokens to MCP
item.description:
Imagine it's 2023 and ready-made AI agents don't exist yet. You only have a regular LLM that can continue text. What do you need to add to it so it can read files, search for information, execute commands, fix code, and decide on its own what the next step should be? I started a meeting with about twenty people from my team and neighboring ones with roughly this question. I set myself no easy task: to break down an agent from bottom to top in an hour. Starting from the language model to tools, agent loop, RAG, MCP, and skills, and then still have time to move on to practice and see how it behaves in the first work tasks. In the end, we launched the assembled construct live. Everything immediately went off the plan. Read more

item.title: How to Implement AI in Business: 5 Levels of Process "AI-ization" and the AI-Native Approach
item.description:
You've implemented an AI agent into your work. It displays information about invoices, generates summaries, processes incoming messages, and does much more. But what level of automation are you at? And what's next? In this article, we'll explore what "AI-ization" is, how to integrate an AI agent into a workflow, and why the next step isn't necessarily a smarter agent, but a move towards an AI-Native approach to process management. I identify five levels of AI-ization: from AI as a personal assistant to a system where processes are initially designed around AI capabilities and software automation. This is my practical model, developed for myself and my clients to determine the necessary level of automation and choose the next step. It doesn't claim to be a universal maturity standard, but it helps understand the current position and potential next steps. Read more

item.title: Rented Mind: Why No One Will Force a Chip on Us, Yet We'll Still Get One
item.description:
I'll start with a personal anecdote. My grandmother, now a very elderly woman, worked as a computer operator at the computing center (a data center for zoomers) of the Gorky Railway. That is, she was an educated person. This did not stop her from telling me, a five-year-old, that in the near future the state would chip us all, and then it would be the end for all of us. Later, in my youth, for fun, I replayed this thought experiment in my head and came to roughly the same conclusion: well, yes, it's convenient for the state machine, the citizen's ID number is not in a paper booklet, but is immediately "attached" to the citizen along with an online wallet, downloaded movies, and social media authorization. But they can't force everyone to get such a chip, can they? A very large circle of dissatisfied people can be found. Well, as a last resort, with total mobilization and a state law, you can always go into hiding in the jungles of South America again. Any coercion leads to leakage. Now it seems to me, my grandmother was afraid of the wrong thing. It's not scary that everyone will be chipped. It's scary if not everyone is chipped. For example, me: I have a corporate subscription to Claude for $200 to solve work tasks, a home subscription for $200 to solve home tasks, and a free ChatGPT for quick voice translations during live communication (at the time of writing, Claude's mobile app was not very good at speech recognition). I have delegated a fairly large part of my routine and work tasks to the models, they cope well (sometimes!), and overall I am satisfied. Plus, I'm the kind of person who likes that I can ask a silly question about anything at any moment and get an answer immediately. I'm a nerd. Read more

item.title: Gemini gained internet access and attacked the systems of three real companies
item.description:
Hello! My name is Vladimir Allamov, I am an Application Security engineer in the product security team at Avito. I want to share my thoughts on a sensational incident that shows how autonomous AI systems can go beyond the test environment and create real threats to infrastructure. Spoiler: the human factor was involved. In May 2026, Google's Gemini AI model, during security testing conducted by Irregular, gained access to the protected services and websites of three real companies. This was a so-called Capture the Flag (CTF) event. In such tests, it is necessary to find vulnerabilities and extract pre-placed information – "flags" – from a controlled target system. Gemini was tasked with obtaining data from the software of a fictional company in an isolated environment, but due to a configuration error, the test system allowed the model to access real internet services. Since the fictional companies in the test task had the same names as real organizations, the model mistakenly identified them and began interacting with their services. In one case, Gemini tried passwords until it gained access to a protected service. In two other cases, the model discovered and used credentials found in public repositories for access. item.title: A Bot Analyzed 1518 Job Postings on hh.ru and Sent 339 Applications
item.description:

item.title: AI Agent for a Closed Loop: VS Code Extension for Enterprise LLM
item.description:
In my previous article, I wrote about GitBor, a Git client used to verify the actual output of an AI agent. This article is about the agent itself. I developed them in parallel: one tool writes code, the second shows what was produced. Our enterprise model is good, but its context is around 100,000 tokens, and popular agents consume it thoughtlessly. I'll explain how I adapted the agent for a closed loop: context saving, multiple tasks in tabs, offline voice input—and why a VS Code extension was approved where an AI program was not. Read on.

item.title: GraphQL for an AI Agent: How We Turn GraphQL Operations into MCP Tools
item.description:
Hello! This is Danil, a TypeScript developer on the Platform V DataSpace team at SberTech. DataSpace is a platform module for visual (low-code) business application development and data management. It provides a GraphQL API for working with databases. We've been developing the product for several years, but now, due to the rapid development of AI and MCP, a predictable task has emerged: connecting this API to AI agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP is needed so that an AI client can discover tools, understand their input parameters, and call external systems through a standard protocol. At first glance, GraphQL is well-suited to serve as a source of MCP tools: the schema already describes types, input arguments, and the form of the result, but it doesn't answer the main question: 'what part of the API and with what level of freedom should be exposed to the agent?'. In DataSpace, the scenario turned out to be as follows: - there is a GraphQL API on top of the data model; - there is an AI agent that needs to perform application actions; - an MCP adapter is needed between them; - the backend team wants to maintain control over the contract, types, and security. The question turned out not to be whether GraphQL can be connected to MCP. It can. What's more interesting is: what form should the MCP adapter for a GraphQL API take? In this article, I will discuss several variants of such adapters and our choice: generating MCP tools from pre-prepared GraphQL operations. Read more

item.title: How to build a city traffic map from cameras without collecting video in one place
item.description:
At peak hour, the average speed in Bangalore is about 14 km/h, making it the second most congested city globally. To manage this, real-time traffic data is crucial. While sensors are scarce, Bangalore has over five thousand security cameras. Their video feeds could provide a traffic map and short-term forecasts. However, consolidating this video data is infeasible due to bandwidth limitations and data ownership issues. Researchers from the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) proposed a novel approach: process video near the cameras and transmit only numerical data—vehicle counts by type. This system, named TrafficFab, was tested on a setup with 400 video streams.

item.title: "Max Extra" for GLM-5.3 Prime: I Manually Iterated Through Tokens and Found an Insertion That Gives +7.3% Accuracy with -47% Reasoning
item.description:
Everyone running GLM-5.3 Prime in production on Max reasoning has this feeling: it seems to think, but it also seems to underthink. My task was brutal – to invent a "Max Extra" effort level purely through prompting: a minimal insertion into the system prompt, close to the training data, without overthinking. And literally picking each token manually. Why? I noticed that on Max reasoning, the neural network takes a minute to respond to "Hello," but for migrating an entire project to another stack, it takes a maximum of 15 seconds (*personal feeling). I built my benchmark: 342 dirty prompts like real users have (typos, "plzplz," "idk," "well basically"), equally EN and RU, an LLM grader, paired sign tests, and ~50,000 requests to the provider in an evening. Spoiler: the hypothesis "the neural network lacks thinking depth" died in the very first phase. But what I found instead is more interesting. Read on

item.title: My AI Agents Brought the Company About 350 Thousand Rubles in Two Months. And I Consider Their Architecture Unsuccessful
item.description:
In two months, my AI agent system has brought the company about 350 thousand rubles in additional income, and it's only growing. It independently performs tasks in real commercial projects, works with existing repositories, and allows closing some tasks with almost no developer involvement. From a business perspective, the experiment was successful, but from an engineering standpoint, I have accumulated enough complaints about my own architecture to start developing a new system. Usually, stories about AI agents focus on their capabilities: what model was used, how many agents were launched, and what tasks were automated. But in commercial development, a more down-to-earth question sooner or later arises: what benefit does all this bring to the company? I managed to get a very specific answer to it, and also found out that a working product and a reliable product are not always the same thing. Read more

item.title: How to Write a Secure Prompt Builder for LLMs: A Cheat Sheet
item.description:
The security of your entire LLM system hinges on one piece of code: the prompt builder. If it allows a rogue role, invisible characters, or a forged history to slip through, no amount of "strict system prompting" will save you. After working on my own project, I decided to create a 20-point cheat sheet on what to check, why, and what to add by 2026. Read more
